questions.stem: The accounting period concept means that:
options: every transaction must be recorded on the same day that cash changes hands with the customer
assets are reported at their original cost rather than their market value
the owner's private transactions are kept separate from the business
the life of a business is divided into equal periods, such as a financial year, for reporting
questions.explanation: Dividing the business's life into periods, commonly 1 July to 30 June, lets profit and position be measured regularly. Recording at historical cost and separating private transactions are other concepts.

questions.stem: How is the going concern principle related to the accounting period concept?
options: because the business will close at the end of each period, all of its assets must be sold on balance day
because each period is independent, the business can ignore any amounts owing from earlier periods
because the business is a going concern, it only needs to report once, when it finally closes
because the business is expected to continue indefinitely, its life must be split into periods to measure performance
questions.explanation: If a business continues indefinitely, owners cannot wait until it ends to know how it performed, so its life is divided into reporting periods. Going concern also justifies carrying items such as prepayments and non-current assets into later periods.

questions.stem: Under accrual accounting, revenue is recognised:
options: at the end of the year, when all customers have paid
when it is earned, whether or not cash has been received
only when cash is received from the customer
when the customer places an order with the business
questions.explanation: Accrual accounting records revenue in the period it is earned and expenses in the period they are incurred. Recording only on receipt of cash is cash accounting.

questions.stem: In the end-of-year reporting process, which step comes immediately before preparing the financial statements?
options: collecting the year's source documents
preparing the adjusted trial balance
recording the reversing entries
recording the opening entry
questions.explanation: After balance day adjustments are recorded, an adjusted trial balance checks the ledger and provides the figures for the statements. Reversing entries are made on the first day of the next period.

questions.stem: Balance day adjustments are made mainly so that:
options: the bank balance in the ledger agrees with the bank statement
all revenue and expense accounts are reset to zero for the next period
errors in the general journal are found and corrected
the period's reports include all revenue earned and expenses incurred in that period
questions.explanation: Balance day adjustments apply accrual accounting so profit for the period is correctly measured. Agreeing the bank balance is the bank reconciliation, and resetting accounts is done by closing entries.

questions.stem: On 1 October, Wren Gardening paid $1,800 for twelve months' insurance and recorded it as Prepaid Insurance. Ignoring GST, what is Insurance Expense for the year ended 30 June?
questions.explanation: October to June is 9 months, so the expense is 1,800 × 9/12 = $1,350. The remaining $450 for July to September is still a prepaid expense, a current asset.

questions.stem: On 1 May, Wren Gardening received $6,000 in advance for six months of garden maintenance, May to October, and recorded it as Unearned Revenue. Ignoring GST, what is the balance day adjustment at 30 June?
options: Dr Bank 6,000; Cr Fees Revenue 6,000
Dr Unearned Revenue 2,000; Cr Fees Revenue 2,000
Dr Fees Revenue 2,000; Cr Unearned Revenue 2,000
Dr Unearned Revenue 4,000; Cr Fees Revenue 4,000
questions.explanation: Two months' work (May and June) has been done, so 6,000 × 2/6 = $2,000 is now earned and moves from the liability to revenue. The other $4,000 remains unearned revenue because the work is still owed.

questions.stem: At 30 June, Wren Gardening has earned $750 of commission from a nursery for referrals in June, to be received in July. Which balance day adjustment is recorded?
options: Dr Accrued Revenue 750; Cr Commission Revenue 750
Dr Commission Revenue 750; Cr Accrued Revenue 750
Dr Bank 750; Cr Commission Revenue 750
Dr Accrued Revenue 750; Cr Bank 750
questions.explanation: The commission was earned in June, so it is recognised as revenue and an asset (accrued revenue) for the amount still to be received. No cash has moved yet, so Bank is not affected.

questions.stem: Wren Gardening forgets to record $1,200 of accrued wages at 30 June. What is the effect on its reports?
options: net profit and current liabilities are both overstated by $1,200
net profit is overstated and current liabilities are understated by $1,200
net profit is understated and current assets are overstated by $1,200 at year end
net profit is correct, but the bank balance is overstated by $1,200
questions.explanation: Leaving out an expense incurred in June makes expenses too low, so profit is too high, and the wages owed are missing from liabilities. No cash has been paid, so the bank balance is correct.

questions.stem: What is the effect of the closing entries at the end of the period?
options: all accounts, including assets and liabilities, start the new period at nil
the balance day adjustments are cancelled for the new period
revenue, expense and drawings accounts have nil balances, and capital is updated
asset and liability accounts have nil balances, and capital is unchanged
questions.explanation: Closing entries transfer revenue and expense balances to a summary account, transfer the profit or loss to capital, and close drawings to capital. Assets and liabilities carry forward, and cancelling adjustments is done by reversing entries.

questions.stem: Why are reversing entries recorded at the start of a new period?
options: so all asset and liability accounts are reset to zero for the new period
so the previous year's net profit is transferred to the owner's capital
so that any errors in last year's statements are automatically corrected
so a later payment or receipt for an accrual can be recorded in full in the normal account
questions.explanation: Reversing an accrual means the next cash payment or receipt can be recorded in the usual way, and the account automatically shows only the new period's share. Transferring profit to capital is done by closing entries.

questions.stem: Accrued electricity of $350 was recorded at 30 June and reversed on 1 July. On 20 July a bill for $900 is paid and debited in full to Electricity Expense. Ignoring GST, what is the balance of Electricity Expense after the payment?
options: $550 debit
$900 debit
$350 credit
$1,250 debit
questions.explanation: The reversing entry credited Electricity Expense with $350; the $900 debit leaves 900 − 350 = $550, the electricity used in July. Without the reversal the account would show $900, part of which belonged to June.

questions.stem: An adjusted trial balance is prepared to:
options: list the amounts customers owe at the end of the period
reconcile the cash at bank account with the bank statement
check that debits equal credits after the balance day adjustments
record the closing entries for revenue and expense accounts
questions.explanation: The adjusted trial balance confirms the ledger still balances once adjustments are posted and provides the figures for the statements. Closing entries and reconciliations are separate steps.

questions.stem: In a sole trader's Statement of Financial Position, the owner's equity section shows:
options: net profit less cost of goods sold
opening capital plus net profit less drawings
opening capital plus drawings less net profit
total assets plus total liabilities
questions.explanation: Closing capital = opening capital + capital contributions + net profit − drawings. Drawings reduce equity, and equity equals assets less liabilities, not assets plus liabilities.

questions.stem: Opening capital was $45,000, net profit was $28,000 and drawings were $15,000. What is closing capital?
questions.explanation: 45,000 + 28,000 − 15,000 = $58,000. Adding drawings instead of deducting them gives $88,000.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how the Statement of Profit or Loss and the Statement of Financial Position are linked?
options: both statements report cash at bank, so they always show the same balance at year end
net profit is reported as a current liability in the Statement of Financial Position
net profit increases owner's equity, so it explains part of the change in the Statement of Financial Position
total revenue in the Statement of Profit or Loss always equals total assets in the Statement of Financial Position
questions.explanation: Profit belongs to the owner, so it adds to capital in the owner's equity section. Revenue does not equal assets, and profit is not a liability.

questions.stem: Which element of the accounting equation is reported as a deduction within owner's equity in the Statement of Financial Position?
options: unearned revenue
drawings
accounts payable
accrued expenses
questions.explanation: Drawings reduce the owner's claim on the business, so they are deducted in the owner's equity section. Accounts payable, accrued expenses and unearned revenue are liabilities.

questions.stem: When preparing a Statement of Cash Flows from the cash at bank ledger account, the debit side of the account shows:
options: expenses incurred, including amounts not yet paid
cash receipts, which become inflows in the statement
cash payments, which become outflows in the statement
revenue earned, including sales made on credit
questions.explanation: Cash at bank is an asset, so receipts are debits and payments are credits. Each entry is classified as operating, investing or financing. Credit sales and unpaid expenses do not appear in the bank account.

questions.stem: Wren Gardening's cash at bank account for the year shows: receipts from customers $84,000; payments to suppliers and employees $61,000; interest paid $1,200; equipment bought $9,000; drawings $15,000; loan received $10,000. What is the net cash from operating activities?
questions.explanation: Operating = 84,000 − 61,000 − 1,200 = $21,800, as interest paid is an operating flow. Equipment is investing, and the loan and drawings are financing. Leaving out interest gives $23,000, and $7,800 is the net increase in cash.

questions.stem: Using the same figures, what is the net increase in cash for the year?
questions.explanation: Net change = operating 21,800 − investing 9,000 + financing (10,000 − 15,000) = $7,800. Treating drawings as an inflow or ignoring them gives a much larger figure.

questions.stem: The purpose of a bank reconciliation is to:
options: record the GST owing to the ATO for the quarter
explain the difference between the cash at bank ledger balance and the bank statement balance
calculate the net profit of the business for the period
close the revenue and expense accounts at the end of the year
questions.explanation: A bank reconciliation identifies items recorded in one record but not yet in the other, such as unpresented cheques or bank fees, and helps detect errors and fraud.

questions.stem: The cash at bank ledger shows a debit balance of $5,200. The bank statement shows bank fees of $25, interest earned of $8 and a direct deposit from a customer of $400, none yet recorded in the ledger. What is the updated ledger balance?
questions.explanation: Updated balance = 5,200 − 25 + 8 + 400 = $5,583. Fees reduce cash, while interest and the direct deposit increase it. Reversing all three gives $4,817.

questions.stem: The updated ledger balance is $5,583. There is an unpresented cheque of $700 and an outstanding deposit of $1,100. What balance should the bank statement show?
questions.explanation: The bank has not yet paid the cheque, so its balance is $700 higher, and it has not received the deposit, so its balance is $1,100 lower: 5,583 + 700 − 1,100 = $5,183. Reversing the adjustments gives $5,983.

questions.stem: Wren Gardening's return on owner's equity is 6%, and a bank term deposit offers 4.5%. Which conclusion is most valid?
options: the term deposit is always the better choice because its return is lower and safer
the business is clearly the better choice because any higher return is worth any risk
the two cannot be compared because the term deposit has no owner's equity
the business earns more, but the margin may not justify its higher risk and the owner's work
questions.explanation: Return on owner's equity can be compared with alternative investments, but the business carries more risk and requires the owner's time, so a small margin may not be enough. Neither option is automatically better.

questions.stem: In March, Wren Gardening's fees revenue was similar to February's, but its net profit fell sharply. What should the owner examine first in the monthly Statement of Profit or Loss?
options: the number of customers on the aged receivables report
which expenses rose between February and March
the closing capital in the Statement of Financial Position
the bank statement balance at the end of March
questions.explanation: If revenue was steady and profit fell, expenses must have risen, so comparing each expense between months shows where. Capital and the bank balance do not explain a change in profit.

questions.stem: Wren Gardening's rent will rise from $2,000 to $2,500 a month. Last year its net profit was $40,000 on revenue of $200,000. If nothing else changes, what is the expected net profit ratio?
questions.explanation: The rise is $500 × 12 = $6,000 a year, so profit falls to $34,000 and 34,000 ÷ 200,000 = 17%. Counting only one month's increase gives 19.75%.

questions.stem: Wren Gardening plans to employ a part-time worker. Which recommendation best reflects an evaluation of the change?
options: hire, because more staff always increases a business's net profit
do not hire, because wages are an expense and expenses always reduce profit
hire, and record the wages as a non-current asset to protect the net profit
hire if the extra jobs the worker allows will earn more than the added wages and on-costs
questions.explanation: The decision depends on whether additional revenue from the extra capacity exceeds the extra costs, including superannuation and other on-costs. Wages are an expense and cannot be recorded as an asset to inflate profit.
